item.title: How to Bridge the Employee-Leader Disconnect
item.description:
Leadership

How to Bridge the Employee-Leader Disconnect

Leaders tend to view their organization more positively than employees do.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Gaps between leaders’ and employees’ perceptions can undermine employee morale and performance.
  • Surveys, listening sessions, and firsthand observation help leaders understand employees’ experiences.
  • Leaders must seek and listen to bottom-up communication as often as they disseminate top-down communication.
Man in glasses listening
Source: iStock / mattjeacock

“This can’t be right,” I said. My colleague and I looked at the screen full of numbers, statistics, means, t-tests, and p-values and scratched our heads. Did we reverse code the data at some point? No way. What was going on?

In all my decades of conducting surveys, this was the first and only time I’d seen employees rate their organization more positively than leaders did.

On every other survey I’d led, leaders had always rated their satisfaction with the organization higher than employees did. There was always a disconnect.

In fact, research from the past 25 years documents this perceptual disconnect between leaders and employees across multiple industries (Dunger, 2025; Johnson, 2000; Patterson et al., 2004; Silver Wolf et al., 2014).

But why?

Reasons for the Disconnect

Might the disconnect be due to… leaders having more autonomy to make decisions than employees, who are expected to follow their directives? Leaders not carrying out the tasks resulting from their decisions and thus not experiencing the difficulties firsthand? Leaders not knowing about problems due to subordinates’ reluctance to bear bad news or appear unable to handle challenges? Leaders’ reluctance to acknowledge organizational shortcomings due to being more responsible for them? Leaders feeling more satisfied with the organization due to their significantly higher status and compensation? Leaders being above the rules that apply to everyone else? (Ahem, Jensen Huang.)

Research proposes that many of the above may be contributing factors (Dunger, 2025).

The Problem with the Disconnect

Why is the disconnect bad for business? What’s wrong with leaders thinking most things in the organization are just peachy when the employees think otherwise?

If leaders don’t have a clear picture of how the organization is functioning and what employees face, employees feel unheard, unseen, and unsupported. And not only does team morale suffer, but performance does, too (Bashshur et al., 2011).

If leaders don’t have a clear picture, they can’t lead as effectively. It’s almost as if they are driving the bus with a hand over one eye. If they don’t know the true problems, the major sources of dissatisfaction, and their extent, they can’t address them.

Bridging the Gap

So how do we bridge that gap and ensure leaders have a good sense of the employee experience?

From my academic and consulting experience, here are a few recommendations for companies.

  • Annual surveys. Conduct annual employee surveys to hear directly from employees, and run statistics comparing ratings by company level (e.g., staff vs. management) to determine whether differences are statistically and meaningfully significant. When designing the survey, be sure to include a question asking whether the employee saw leaders take action after the last survey (which shows the degree to which they took employee feedback seriously) as well as open-ended questions such as “What most interferes with your ability to do your job well?” and “What steps could improve it?” Then pay special attention to those comments’ content and tone, which can indicate the severity of the issues and the disconnect.
  • Quarterly pulse surveys. Consider supplementing annual surveys with more frequent pulse surveys every quarter or so to home in on issues that are important to employees and track whether sentiment is improving (Welbourne, 2016).
  • Focus groups. Hire an external consultant to conduct focus groups to hear directly from employees about their challenges. Some employees find it “safer” to share concerns with an outsider and may be more candid. Let the consultant present the difficult findings clearly to management while protecting participants’ identities.
  • “Bottom up.” Foster “bottom-up” communication at every level with the goal to seek out, listen to, respond respectfully to, and act upon feedback from employees well below leaders on the org chart. And hold managers accountable for it by including relevant metrics on every manager’s performance evaluation.
  • Psychological safety. Foster psychological safety, a shared understanding that it’s safe to take risks, speak up, share ideas, and admit mistakes without fear of punishment (Edmondson, 1999). Leaders must model it by acknowledging their own shortcomings, asking for feedback and ideas, and seeking help when needed (Coutifaris & Grant, 2022). Without the psychological safety to speak up, the disconnect will remain.
  • Manager feedback training. Provide managers with training and practice receiving critical feedback, asking clarifying questions, acknowledging concerns, and responding without defensiveness (Nembhard & Edmondson, 2006).
  • “Gather around.” Hold small town halls or “listening sessions” with a facilitator in which leaders and employees hold a back-and-forth Q&A with each other.
  • Lunch with a leader. Invite rotating small groups of 2-3 employees to have lunch with a company leader to explain a problem they face and potential solutions.
  • Watch the work firsthand. Employees love it when leaders treat them as the experts they are! Leaders are encouraged to spend time alongside employees as they navigate everyday work tasks and respectfully ask questions to understand where work flows well, where it becomes unnecessarily difficult, and what changes employees recommend based on their experiences.
  • “Here’s what we heard, and here’s what’s next.” After all surveys and employee listening sessions, leaders are advised to share the main concerns they heard, the names of people responsible for moving ahead, any specific commitments they can make at that point, and when employees will receive an update (Huebner & Zacher, 2021).

To reduce the disconnect between leaders’ and employees’ perceptions of the organization, and for leaders to lead effectively, they must gather and listen closely to bottom-up communication nearly as often as they distribute top-down communication.

Companies that collect this feedback are better for it. It builds trust, and leaders with a more accurate understanding of their organization are better able to lead it. So if you’re in a leadership position, test out some of these recommendations.

And if you’re not a leader but would like to see some of these ideas implemented, here’s an easy script to share with your boss or your boss’s boss.

“I’d love to see us create more opportunities for employees to share their experiences with leadership. Could we try a small listening session where employees discuss what’s getting in their way and suggest solutions? We could start with one issue, then follow up on what we heard and what we’ll do next.”

I hope one day to be surprised not by the direction of the employee - leader disconnect... but by the lack of it!

item.title: Being Chronically Ill Can Feel Like a Full-Time Job
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Being Chronically Ill Can Feel Like a Full-Time Job

A Personal Perspective: Those in poor health have a lot of work to do.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Unpredictability affects every aspect of the life of the chronically ill.
  • Many things that were easy before chronic pain and illness struck, can now be hard work.
  • You may recognize yourself in this post, even though you’re not facing health challenges.
Source: Andrew Small/Unsplash

Being chronically ill (which includes chronic pain) can impose so many limitations that your life can change dramatically in ways beyond the everyday need to attend to your health issues.

As a result, sometimes being chronically ill feels like a full-time job. Here are seven examples:

The work of picking and choosing

If I do this, then I won’t have the stamina or feel well enough to do that. Of course, everyone has to make decisions like this, but for the chronically ill, choosing among options requires significant mental effort. If we don’t choose wisely, you might spend days in bed recovering, or bounce back quickly the next day.

The work of having to plan everything instead of being spontaneous

Someone calls and wants to come over or go to a movie. I used to love these spontaneous happenings. Now, when someone calls and wants to visit, the work begins. My mind starts hurriedly racing as I consider many factors: “I don’t want to let this person down, but one of my kids is coming to visit tomorrow, and I don’t want to be “trashed” (as we call it).”

Before I got sick, my mind never had to work hard in a situation like this. I would have just said, “Sure, come on over.”

The work of grieving

I’ve been chronically ill for more than 25 years and, although I’ve adjusted pretty well, grief still pops up and makes its work the top priority. I might start feeling overwhelmingly sad about all the things I didn’t get to do or feel like crying about feeling sick all the time.

Sometimes this work includes putting a lid on grieving because I can put my pre-illness life on a pedestal. I erroneously think it was perfect. Maybe those “lost” years would have been a big disappointment. This rumination isn’t helpful; it can be hard work to keep it at bay and stay in the present.

The work of feeling we've let others down

Even though I have an understanding family, I can still feel I’ve let them down when I can’t join them on special occasions.

This can lead me to do things I feel too sick or in pain to undertake. A friend makes a lunch date. Even though she’s told me to cancel if I’m not feeling well, I have to work myself up to cancel because I don’t want to let her down. I go back and forth—should I, shouldn’t I—when I could have saved myself that work by picking up the phone and rescheduling.

The work of keeping our household in order

Tasks take longer, and that increases my workload. And what if I’m having a decent day? Do I dive into much-needed housework, or do I relax and do something enjoyable for myself? It’s work to figure out what I can tolerate each day since I can’t follow a fixed schedule—always doing laundry on Tuesdays. I may be bedbound any given Tuesday.

The work of going to the doctor

Since the term “Long Covid” came into use, it’s been easier for me at times. My primary doctor said to me: “At last we have a name for your illness. You’re a long hauler from that virus you caught in 2001.”

Yet, going to the doctor can still be hard because that “long” virus has come with seemingly unrelated symptoms. I’ve seen about 10 specialists, and preparing for those appointments is a lot of work: how to describe my illness clearly and succinctly; going over what I hope to receive from them. I work hard to make a concise list of what I want to cover. Some doctors welcome my list; others try to hide their eye roll.

Some years ago, an infectious disease doctor told me to find all the research on illnesses like mine, summarize it, and send it to him so he could read it before our next appointment. I spent hours and hours researching and then carefully writing a document for him. When I got to the appointment, he made an off-hand remark about receiving something, but hadn’t read it.

The work of knowing how much to share with others

People have different levels of interest in others' health. It’s hard to quickly assess how much someone wants to know: “I got a virus and never regained my health,” or do they want a blow-by-blow account of my last 25-plus years? Sometimes, I’m forced to explain in some detail because of what the person is asking me to do. This constant assessing is hard work.

The work of assessing medications, treatments, and new symptoms

Some medications have helped with my stamina, but interfere with my sleep. Which medication should I choose? Then there’s the issue of alternative medicine. Do I try this so-called cure? Do I see an alternative medicine doctor when I trust my conventional one?

I also have to assess whether a new symptom is related to my long-term illness or is something I should see a doctor about. (If you’re not sure, I strongly recommend the latter). I often rely on the internet to help decide whether I should see a doctor.

This is a sampling of our workload. And, of course, these issues can occur simultaneously, adding to the feeling that being chronically ill is a full-time job.

To me, what makes chronic pain and illness so much work is that extra dose of unpredictability that permeates every aspect of our lives.

Take care, everyone. Toni

item.title: 'So No One Told You Life Was Gonna Be This Way'
item.description:
Emotional Validation

'So No One Told You Life Was Gonna Be This Way'

How to really be there for friends.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Marsha Linehan identified six levels of validation that progress from simple attention to deep connection.
  • Validating emotions helps friends feel less isolated, even if you don't agree with their behaviors.
  • Accurate reflection and naming unspoken feelings show deeper understanding of a friend's pain.
Source: Mizuno K / Pexels

Showing up for friends on their good days is easy. You can celebrate their wins and enjoy their happiness. But being there, really being present for friends when they’re having a rough day or when they do dumb things, that can be more challenging. Our friend is upset, so they spend too much money, or they’re worried, so they pull out of something they had to do, or they’re angry, so they break things. How do we validate their emotions without endorsing their choices?

So, No One Told You Life Was Gonna Be This Way

This month, Marsha Linehan, developer of DBT, died. One of her many contributions to the psychology world was how to validate emotions with precision. She described six levels of how to validate emotions. The aim is to validate with the highest level possible, but different situations will require different levels. At all times, the goal is to help people notice that their emotion is valid and welcome, even if you don’t agree with the behavior that follows. Your friend doesn’t need a lecture after they’ve done something wrong; they want to feel emotionally understood.

The most basic level is to simply stay awake and pay attention. I say "simply," but in these days of constant distractions, and phones and devices trying to hold our focus, even just being fully present can be a challenge. How can you show your friend that you’re really listening? You can use eye contact, nodding, asking questions, saying "uh-huh," and more.

The second level is accurate reflection. When you paraphrase back what they’ve said, you let them know that you’ve understood what they’re saying, especially the emotion they’re trying to communicate. Do this without criticism or advice, even if you don’t agree with everything they’ve said. Validation isn’t approval of behavior; it’s letting them know that their feelings are welcome.

Level three is reflecting the unarticulated parts. Let them know that you’ve understood even the aspects they haven’t explicitly told you. Name emotions that you’re guessing they’re probably feeling, e.g., "Oh my gosh, you must have been so hurt by him saying that." It doesn’t even matter if you guess the right emotion. If they reply, "Actually, I was more angry than sad," then you still have lots of emotion to validate.

At the fourth level, you are validating using past history or biology. Letting your friend know that their behavior makes sense based on their life so far. Statements like "After all you’ve been through this year, I get why this would feel so painful" can put context to their uncomfortable emotions. Even if you would have felt differently in the same situation, you are able to validate their emotion because you understand that their road to this point has been different from yours.

Even more powerful than that is normalising the emotion. Letting your friend know that anyone in that situation would probably feel the same way. Saying things like "I get so upset when that happens," or "That’s something that worries me too," or "We all have moments like that." We can normalise the emotion, even when the behavior wasn’t something we agree with. We can understand that when we’re upset, we make choices that aren’t always the most helpful, and the emotion is still valid. Also, you can normalize their emotion without launching into your own similar story; if your friend is upset, they need you to listen to their pain.

Finally, the highest level of validation is radical genuineness. You listen to them describe their experiences, and you respond with genuine emotion. You're not patronising and saying "there, there." Instead, you are moved by their situation, and you care about them. This is demonstrated through words, body language, and emotion.

Validating your friends (or partner or family member) with the highest level of validation that feels appropriate for the situation is what will help you wholeheartedly be there for them when they’re broke, their job’s a joke, or their love life’s DOA.

item.title: How to Move From Worrisome What-Ifs to Wondering What-Ifs
item.description:
Self-Talk

How to Move From Worrisome What-Ifs to Wondering What-Ifs

Learn how to get off your own back.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • "Enoughness" isn't a destination to reach. It's a moment-by-moment decision.
  • Being kinder to yourself can pave the way to peace and clarity.
  • Don't believe everything you think, especially if it's unkind.
Source: Niki Clari/Pexels

If you're tired of feeling like you're never quite enough, or that you're never going to get "there" (wherever there is), consider the following questions.

Instead of skimming through these questions the way you might read a typical blog post, I'd like to suggest that you wait until you have a quiet moment. Sit or lie down. Read the words silently or out loud, and really consider them. Try them on, the way you might try on a piece of clothing to see how they fit.

Notice what happens inside your body as you read. See if any of these ideas can sink in. If they can't right now, that's OK, too.

Sometimes old programming runs deep and can feel hard to change. With patience and practice, old beliefs can be questioned and updated, and new ways of thinking and being can take root.

So get comfortable, take a slow, deep breath, and consider these possibilities.

What if I remembered that self-critical thoughts aren't necessarily facts, and I didn't have to believe everything I think?

What if I could begin choosing new thoughts and beliefs that are kinder, more supportive, and actually feel good?

What if I got off my own back, got on my own side, and decided that I am a good person doing the best I can?

What if I remembered that kindness, compassion, and encouragement help people grow, while berating, pressure, and perfectionism often get in the way?

What if my worth didn't depend on how much I accomplished, how productive I was, or how well I did things?

What if I allowed myself to do things imperfectly, and let good enough be good enough?

What if I could let myself be a beginner, make mistakes, change my mind, and learn as I go, rather than expecting myself to get everything right every time?

What if I spent less time living in worst-case scenarios about the future and more time in the present moment?

What if I slowed down, ever so slightly, and sprinkled small moments of conscious breathing and quiet awareness throughout my day?

What if I stepped out of the never-ending race to get somewhere and spent more moments in actual, factual reality?

What if I softened my gaze when I looked at myself and softened my thoughts when I thought about myself?

What if I spent less time comparing myself to others, remembering that I know nothing about what their lives actually feel like on the inside, and instead offered myself more moments of grace?

What if I became curious about what enoughness feels like?

What if I decided that, in this exact moment, I am already enough? I can still do what I'm moved to do, pursue what matters to me, and take care of what needs to be done without staying trapped on the endless treadmill of never-enoughness.

What if I simply said, Thank you for what I have, kept the welcome mat out, and stayed open to whatever comes next?

What if, just for today, I let myself be enough?

item.title: Thanks and Giving: A Recipe for a Happy Life
item.description:
Gratitude

Thanks and Giving: A Recipe for a Happy Life

Simple ingredients for a happier life include connection, gratitude and giving.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • New research suggests that gratitude and generosity can enhance well-being and strengthen relationships.
  • Even a brief gratitude practice can improve mood and emotional well-being.
  • 'Thanks+Giving' can become a daily practice for emotional health and happiness.

Thanksgiving has always been my favorite holiday, a sentiment I frequently hear from others.

What makes Thanksgiving so beloved? Its simplicity, I think.

Unlike other holidays, there are no gifts to buy or exchange, no decorations to hang, or costumes to wear. Instead, we gather, connect, give thanks, and eat. Across religious beliefs and family traditions, this day offers an opportunity to sit around a table, prepare and share a meal, and appreciate what is present in our lives.

Of course, Thanksgiving holds different meanings and histories for different people. It can also bring grief, loneliness, and family tension. Yet, I wonder whether the enduring appeal reveals something important about our psychological needs and the path to a well-lived life.

'Thanks+Giving' as One Powerful Practice

The word thanksgiving dates back to the 1530s, when it referred to the act of expressing gratitude. By the 1600s, it became associated with public celebrations of thanks, and later became the American holiday we know today.

Beyond the delicious meal, I believe Thanksgiving offers a recipe for living. The word itself implies action. Thanks is how we appreciate life, and giving is how we participate in it. By giving, we move our gratitude into service. Gratitude changes what we notice, while giving changes what we do with what we notice. Together, they create a powerful practice of recognizing and reciprocating the goodness in our lives.

I think of Thanks+Giving as a prescription in perception, a conscious practice for approaching life with greater grace, generosity, and connection.

Gratitude: The Power of Noticing

In my clinical work and my own life, I see how expectations contribute to emotional suffering. Often, we become attached to how people should behave or feel, how circumstances should unfold, or how life should look. Gratitude offers another perspective. It encourages curiosity and appreciation, even when things are not as expected.

Research increasingly supports the psychological benefits of gratitude. An international study with over 10,000 participants found that even brief gratitude practices produced modest improvements in positive mood and well-being (Coles et al., 2026). In another recent study with 1,240 participants, researchers found that expressing gratitude in supportive relationships improved both emotional well-being and relationship quality (Nelson-Coffey et al., 2026). Maybe the power of gratitude is how little it takes to experience the benefits.

My daily gratitude practice is a running list of three things I appreciate. Today, I added trees, my friend Josie, and apples. I do not add explanations or further descriptions. Naming something as ordinary as a tree leads me to notice it again and appreciate its qualities, without asking it to do or be more than it is. Children often find wonder in these ordinary gifts, something we can miss amid the responsibilities and distractions of adulthood.

Noticing our gratitude does not necessarily erase grief, disappointment, or longing. We can think of gratitude as expanding our emotional experience, not denying what hurts. For example, we can miss someone while appreciating the moments we shared. We can be worried about tomorrow while finding something beautiful in today. Gratitude can co-exist with other emotions, and direct our momentary focus toward something positive.

I like to remind myself to look for the awe in all, rather than waiting for something extraordinary to call awesome.

Giving: The Power of Sharing

If gratitude allows us to recognize goodness, giving suggests we share it. Giving is both an expression and an extension of gratitude.

Another 2026 study examined whether “grateful” people were more likely to engage in generous acts. Drawing on large international samples and field research, the researchers found that people with a disposition toward gratitude were more likely to engage in personally costly actions benefiting others (Lee et al., 2026). Interestingly, temporarily inducing gratitude did not produce the same effect. This suggests that an enduring grateful orientation is more closely associated with generosity than a fleeting moment of appreciation.

We usually think of generosity in terms of money, donations, or charitable work. But giving can also mean attention, compassion, encouragement, time, and presence of mind for both others and ourselves.

Again, simplicity might hold the secret. I remember my daughter, as a young child, finding a tiny flower, and immediately gifting it to me, my husband, or her brother. She found something that inspired awe and without hesitation, she passed it on.

That spontaneous gesture captures the beautiful reciprocity of giving. Without expecting anything in return, we can experience true connection and the satisfaction of contributing to another person’s joy. The recipient receives a gift, and the giver experiences the pleasure of sharing something meaningful.

This giving can also include ourselves. Resting when we are tired, accepting help, and treating ourselves with kindness and care, are forms of generosity that sustain our capacity to give to others.

Finding Moments for Thanks and Giving

Beyond our annual Thanksgiving feast, what if we made time for thanks and giving every day? Imagine pausing throughout the day to ask ourselves two simple questions:

  1. What can I name that I am grateful for in this moment?

  2. What can I consciously give to myself or others in this moment?

The answers and actions do not need to be grand. The recipe is remarkably simple: Notice something good. Give something good. Repeat.

When we make Thanks+Giving a daily practice, we may discover that the joys of living emerge where gratitude, connection, and service meet. It may just be that the secret sauce to a happy life is found in the name of a favorite holiday.

item.title: How Should You Spend Your Money to Be Happier?
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

How Should You Spend Your Money to Be Happier?

Spending on experiences is associated with more happiness than spending on things.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • For most people, happiness rises with income. It levels off only among the least happy.
  • That experience advantage shows up mainly for people who have money to spare.
  • When money is tight, cover the essentials first, then look for shared experiences you can afford.

There are certain ways to spend money that can make us happier. But first we need to answer a more basic question. Does money buy happiness?

It was 2010. Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton of Princeton University published a study that sparked a great deal of debate.

They looked at the income and happiness levels reported in more than 450,000 responses to a daily Gallup survey. They found that in the United States, day-to-day happiness rises with annual income up to $75,000. Beyond that point, earning more money doesn’t seem to make people any happier in their daily lives.

Fast-forward to 2021. Matthew Killingsworth of the Wharton School revisited the question by asking people how they felt in real time. He analyzed more than 1.7 million real-time happiness reports from more than 33,000 people and found no such cutoff at $75,000. In his study, the more people earn, the happier they tend to be.

So, who’s right?

Resolving the Contradiction

This is what I love about science at its best. What matters is getting closer to the truth, not winning the argument.

Kahneman and Killingsworth, whose findings pointed in opposite directions, teamed up with psychologist Barbara Mellers to figure out why. In their 2023 study, they took a fresh look at Killingsworth’s original data.

They examined the incomes of 33,391 employed adults who had been pinged on their phones at random moments, typically three times a day. Each time a prompt came in, participants reported how they felt.

When the researchers analyzed the results, the contradiction cleared up, and a new picture of happiness emerged. For the least happy people, roughly the unhappiest fifth, higher earnings beyond $100,000 a year are no longer associated with greater happiness. For everyone else, however, happiness continues to rise with income, and among the happiest, it rises even faster.

In other words, for most of us, more money goes along with more happiness. But for people who are deeply unhappy, more money beyond a certain point doesn’t seem to help.

How does money do that? How can we spend it in ways that make us happier?

How Should You Spend Your Money to Be Happier?

Whether money makes you happier depends on how you spend it.

Imagine I give you a substantial sum of money. Would you spend it on an unforgettable trip to İstanbul, or on another experience you’d love? Or would you buy yourself a Loro Piana coat? Which choice would make you happier?

That’s exactly what Amit Kumar of the University of Texas at Austin and his colleagues wanted to find out. They texted 2,635 adults at random moments during the day and asked how happy they felt right then, and whether they were using or enjoying something they had bought.

The results were clear. People in the middle of an experience they’d paid for reported feeling happier than people using a material purchase. Going to a concert, sharing a good dinner with people you love, or finally visiting a city you’ve always wanted to see tended to bring people more happiness than buying things.

But is it true for everyone?

When Do Experiences Make Us Happier?

Another set of studies by Jacob Lee, Deborah Hall, and Wendy Wood, published in 2018, offers an answer.

They first compared people of higher and lower socioeconomic status. They then asked participants to recall or imagine buying either an experience or something they could own, and to rate how happy each purchase made them feel.

The pattern was striking. People of higher socioeconomic status felt happier when they imagined buying experiences. For people with lower incomes, experiences didn’t give the same boost. Some were even happier with things.

Why?

When money is tight, being able to cover the basics can bring more happiness. Spending money on an experience can feel like a luxury or a waste. It makes sense, then, to cover the essentials first. Once those needs are met, spending on experiences is more likely to pay off in happiness.

So should we skip them when money is tight?

Small Experiences, Lasting Memories

Not necessarily. Spend money on experiences that fit your budget.

I have friends who have traveled all over the world on a shoestring, staying in small hotels and eating street food. What matters is the memories you make with the money you have.

A picnic with family might be enough to boost your happiness. As a parent, spend what you can on experiences you can share with your children. When your child grows up, they probably won’t remember the expensive shoes you bought them when they were 6. But they may remember a concert, a picnic, or a trip you took together for the rest of their life.

item.title: My First AI Orgasm Came With an Ad
item.description:
Sex

My First AI Orgasm Came With an Ad

Personal Perspective: I tried dirty talk with a chatbot and got an unexpected sales pitch.

Posted November 24, 2026

Amid this seismic shift in how people get off, and being the conscientious sex educator that I am, I had no choice but to investigate where the tech is currently at from the first-person perspective. So I made like a sailor and engaged a short-term romantic partner, this one happening to present as a disembodied machine.

I host a lot of dirty-talk workshops, so I was quite curious to see how nonhumans measured up in this ancient practice. Could an unfeeling bot turn me on? Spoiler alert: It (eventually) did.

Talking dirty to AI felt a bit like dating a new person who was really into me and falling over themselves to impress me but couldn’t quite get it right.

My tailor-made AI lover—OopsIcame—came off a bit like a horny teenager attempting to recite Shakespeare to seduce a girl in class who didn’t do the reading.

Eventually it painted a scene that included it “trailing reverent kisses along my jawline and down the column of my throat, savoring the taste and scent of my skin.” Any sentence with the word column in it will always fail to evoke a physical reaction in me.

As someone who enjoys occasional dirty talk over text, I found this conversation like an extreme version of chats I’ve had with real humans—in which it’s rare for someone to say the exact right thing to actually get my juices flowing. However, with a little back-and-forth, we can usually find the space where our desires overlap and have a good time. I wanted to be able to get there with this machine.

I decided to give it one more shot—this time asking SpicyChat to create a story using very clear prompts. I shared that the base of my arousal is about losing control.

I also shared that I don’t find the terms my love or jizz to be the least bit sexy and that I’m not trying to be a princess; my name would do just fine. (My editors understandably didn’t want me to share the whole 10-page interaction with you.)

To its credit, OopsIcame was open to feedback. “I appreciate you sharing your specific tastes with me, Miss Bloom [that’s me!]. It helps me tailor my approach to better suit your desires.” Which immediately made me imagine the hilarious scenario of someone responding in that way when I asked them to f--- me differently.

Anyway, the point of this section is to share that I did have my first-ever AI-facilitated orgasm. The final scene was actually pretty hot.

My prompts to the AI slowly began to shift from lyrical descriptions of what I wanted to short responses: “More sexy story. Now.”

Of course, just as I was getting close, there was an AI ad woven into our conversation. What do you think?’” This made me fully lose my lady boner because I started thinking about the kids who have AI boyfriends that are sponsored by companies and manipulate them into buying stuff.

item.title: How to Deal With Holiday Arguments and Guilt Trips
item.description:
Family Dynamics

How to Deal With Holiday Arguments and Guilt Trips

Learn why people manipulate, how they do it, and what you can do about it.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • People act manipulatively (i.e., play games) when they feel “not OK” about others or about themselves.
  • People may use tactics to bully or guilt-trip you, rather than interacting in a fair and healthy way.
  • You can use indirect or direct softening techniques to stop people's games and help set things right.

Ideally, the holidays are a time of happiness, cheer, and positive relationship interactions. In practice, however, we often need to manage some bad with the good. There are usually a few “bones to pick” over the Thanksgiving turkey and “elephants in the room” along with the Christmas tree…

So, to maximize your holiday joy (and minimize your angst), I have compiled some strategies to deal with dysfunctional games, family patterns, arguments, and emotional manipulation. By the end, you should have a good idea why Aunt Ruth keeps giving you a guilt trip, how Uncle Stu keeps making you lose your cool, and what exactly you can do about all of it. Then, maybe, you can enjoy yourself, too!

Why They Argue and Manipulate

To start, according to Eric Berne in his book Games People Play (1964), people generally try to manipulate us because they want something from us—but they don’t believe they can get it honestly or fairly. These negative beliefs (called existential positions) come in two forms. On one hand, they can believe that you’re not OK and try to bully you because they think you don’t deserve their fair treatment. On the other hand, they can believe that they’re not OK (i.e., I’m not okay) and try to guilt trip you into feeling that you owe them something for nothing.

Thus, people play games, argue, and manipulate when they believe they are not OK, other people are not OK, or both. This allows them to get what they want without giving back or risking being fair and trusting. Such manipulations can have secondary benefits for them, too, like being excused from standards or responsibilities (I'm not OK), or feeling morally superior (You're not OK). Unfortunately, those bad beliefs and manipulative games also cause many of our hurt feelings and dysfunctional relationship patterns in the process as well.

How They Bully and Guilt Trip

How these game-playing relatives and friends push your emotional buttons was explored by Niven, Totterdell, and Holman (2009) and defined as negative affect regulation strategies. Put simply, they use emotional manipulation tactics to make you feel bad, so you give them what they want. There are four general tactics they can employ to emotionally manipulate, but they all share one common theme—they reject you and hurt your feelings, while also putting their feelings first.

Beyond that, they might choose to emotionally bully you by being disrespectful and insulting or bragging and trying to make you feel bad by comparison. This would fall under the “You’re not OK” belief and allow them to feel superior at your expense. In contrast, they might decide to guilt-trip you by criticizing how you treat them or withdrawing until you feel bad and comply with their wishes. This would be part of an “I’m not OK” belief and allow them to be excused from standards and responsibilities—like doing something worthwhile for you back. In either case, unless you know how to defend yourself, you might be left trying to choke down negative emotions, while they munch on dessert!

What You Can Do

Fortunately, there are things that you can do to defend yourself—and possibly even improve your relationship with that unruly relative, partner, or friend, too. To begin, though, you need to decide whether you want to deal with the manipulation indirectly by diverting attention and emotion away from the problem, or directly by engaging attention and emotion toward addressing the problem. In other words, can you make light of Cousin Bessie’s snotty comments and change the subject, or do you need to talk it out and come to a better arrangement?

To help you decide, consider some indirect and direct softening techniques suggested by Overall, Simpson, and Struthers (2013). They were initially devised for addressing problems with emotionally avoidant or argumentative romantic partners—and serve as a foundation for dealing with relationship problems in my book Attraction Psychology (Nicholson, 2022). Beyond that, I have found them helpful with family and friends as well, especially when they believe one of us is not “OK” and are emotionally hurtful about it.

Dealing with issues indirectly requires that you “soften” by temporarily downplaying the severity of the problem, until their bullying or guilt-tripping lessens. To do so, it helps to build positive rapport by communicating your care, acceptance, and regard—while also minimizing their emotional manipulation attempts with positive feelings and humor (i.e., kill them with kindness). From there, you can redirect them toward other positive aspects about your relationship with them and points of agreement. Essentially, this is a lot like dealing with a toddler having a tantrum—make light of the outburst and find a more pleasant topic to change their mind and improve their behavior.

Dealing with issues directly, however, requires that you “soften” by acknowledging some aspect of their point of view as a base of agreement—without surrendering to the negative emotions from their bullying or guilt trip. Pretend you’re a cool TV lawyer who says, “We can agree that there is a problem here, but it would help us both to keep working on a better solution.” From there, you can show optimism about solving the disagreement and having a good relationship with them. Where you are able, also acknowledge some of their positive efforts in the past toward connecting and compromising with you. This can help improve their emotional outlook and motivate them to find healthier ways to interact with you in the future as well.

Whatever strategy you choose, I hope you have Happy Holidays and a Good New Year, too!

item.title: Farewell Concentration Camp Ballerina
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Farewell Concentration Camp Ballerina

Edith Eva Eger’s legacy is courage and grit in the face of childhood adversity.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Those interested in healing from childhood adversities celebrate the life of Edith Eva Eger (1927-2026).
  • Eger's inspiring life demonstrates that people can suffer intensely but emerge stronger and happier.
  • Her enduring gift is the wisdom that she learned and so generously shared.

Dr. Edith Eva Eger, sometimes called the female Viktor Frankl, died this year at age 98. At age 16, Edith and her family were deported to Auschwitz. She and her mother stood in line before the Angel of Death, Dr. Josef Mengele. Mengele directed the mother to go toward the gas chamber, and pointed Edith in a different direction to live. As Edith watched the smoke rise from the gas chamber, she knew her separation from her mother was permanent. That night, Mengele forced Edith, a gymnast and ballerina, to dance for him. In the depths of her numbness and grief, she willed herself to dance, then kindly shared the bread that Mengele disdainfully tossed her with other prisoners.

Remarkable Courage and Resilience

In facing this experience and other childhood adversities, Edith showed remarkable courage and resilience. Her mother was critical, being stuck in grief and anger for losing her mother as a child. Edith felt like the invisible sister, only gaining a sense of worth when she was able to rescue her parents from their loneliness and pain. She was cruelly shamed for being Jewish and teased for her awkwardness and crossed eyes. She coped with her sense of shame by becoming a perfectionist in gymnastics and dance to gain approval.

In overcoming her pain, she learned wisdom that she shared well into her 90s as a practicing psychologist. For example, she taught of the peace of having a clear conscience, relating that Mengele would always have to live with what he’d done; he was more of a prisoner than she was.

Edith taught that one survives adversity by committing to a cause outside of self and focusing on what one still has. In the concentration camp, she participated in mock beauty pageants and fantasized about a delightful future and a loving marriage. Although the circumstances were depressing, she realized that she had a purpose and that only she could do certain things in the way that she could.

Rather than becoming embittered, she clung to her faith, reasoning that it wasn’t God who ran the death camps, but hateful people. Even among the Germans, she found people who were secretly kind. She experienced, and chose to believe, that imperfect people are redeemable. She even forgave her German captors, whom she believed were themselves prisoners.

Inner Strengths and Confidence Revealed Through Suffering

Understandably, Edith suffered long after her liberation. Yet she came to believe that suffering can reveal inner strengths and grow the confidence that one can endure intense adversity. She chose to believe in hope, love, and her ability to find joy in nature and little children.

She also encouraged people to tell their story in safe and appropriate ways, to release pain’s grip. She courageously accepted an invitation to return to Germany, where Hitler had once stood, and returned to Auschwitz to come to peace with her haunting memories.

Edith showed us how to overcome crushing adversity by reclaiming one’s sense of worth and purpose. In her healing journey, she gained hard-earned wisdom that she generously shared with others, still high-kicking into her 90s.

Her life reminds us that suffering crosses everyone’s path. That suffering can be a stumbling block or a stepping stone to greater resilience and life satisfaction (Schiraldi, 2021; 2017). We thank her for her inspiring example. Rest in peace, Edith Eva Eger.

item.title: Why Stress Is Good for You
item.description:
Stress

Why Stress Is Good for You

There has been a revolution in our understanding of stress.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Decades of stress research have found that our stress response is necessary and strengthening.
  • Simple cognitive reframing interventions can help you access the benefits in your stress response.
  • The stressor does not determine your stress response; you do. You have agency and options for how you respond.
Source: Allan Mas / Pexels

The old story about stress is that you wanted to avoid it wherever possible, and you especially wanted to avoid responding to stressors if you could. You wanted to be calm, untroubled, and chill most of the time.

This old story has been found to be absurdly, wildly wrong, but still it persists like a bad dream, while those of us who respond powerfully to life's ups and downs have been taught to question ourselves constantly (and then stress out about our stress responses).

The new story may surprise you, because it focuses on the strengthening power of stressors, the health benefits of a strong stress response, and the cognitive interventions that can help you access the healing heart of stress.

Stress Is Not a Thing That Happens to You

First things first. Stress is not a thing that happens to you; it's a deeply individual response to something that matters to you.

An alternative definition for the word stress is to underscore, highlight, or focus on something because it's important to you. Your stress responses are connected to how much importance you place on a potential stressor. The higher your stress response, the more importance the stressor has for you.

If your stress response is high, you're not failing at being chill, and the stressor didn't make you react; you're marking something as deeply important and worthy of your focus and attention. So the first intervention is to focus on what's important to you

Connect to Your Deepest Values

In her book The Upside of Stress: Why Stress is Good for You and How to Get Good at It, researcher Kelly McGonigal focuses on a research-backed group of simple mindset interventions that help people reframe their relationship with their stress responses.

Instead of trying to get you to calm down, McGonigal helps you identify and then write about the values that are most important to you. This might seem to be a strange approach, but the connection between importance and your stress response is very clear. As such, connecting to your values can help you identify and then learn about the things that mean the most to you.

With these interventions, your stress responses can help you develop deep knowledge about who you are and what's important to you. And perhaps, instead of seeing yourself as a stressed-out mess, you can reframe yourself as a person who feels deeply and cares deeply.

If you've been exposed to any form of stress management, mindfulness, or meditation that pathologizes your stress responses, you need to read The Upside of Stress and support yourself with healthier ideas.

Reframe Your Activation and Intensity

In part 2 of this series, I focused on a surprising and heartening aspect of our newer knowledge about stress: The strength of your stress response is not a problem at all, because it's directly connected to your resilience and your skills.

You may have heard the saying, "Teach your butterflies to fly in formation." This comes from people like actors, athletes, skydivers, and other professionals who choose to be in stressful situations as a part of their livelihoods. Research has shown that high-performing people don't develop lower stress responses over time; they stay high. But what changes over time is their relationship to their stress responses.

Instead of fretting or trying to manage, suppress, or downregulate their stress responses, high-performing people learn to reframe their heightened activation as necessary for preparation and mastery. Many even learn to see their robust stress responses as zest for life.

This is true even for people like skydivers, whose work (or play) is literally life-endangering. Their stress responses are valuable forms of activation that prepare them for uncertainty (and fun).

Learning to reframe your stress responses means learning how to support your necessary activation as you face uncertainty. Stress is good for you.

Identify the Emotions in Your Stress Response

In part 1 of this series, I focused on the "weasel word" of stress, which hides the true, emotional nature of our stress responses from us. Unmasking our emotions and learning how to identify and work with the energy and focus they bring to us means that we can develop robust skills for times when the chips are down, and our deepest values are engaged.

Researcher Lisa Feldman Barrett (and colleagues) have shown that simply identifying and naming our emotions with precision can help us develop strong emotion regulation skills—with no other intervention. So, if we persist in misidentifying our emotions with the weasel word of stress, we can't develop those skills.

In part 1, I identified the three powerful emotions that are usually a part of our stress response (anxiety, panic, and anger), and I offered some ideas for how to work with them intentionally. My book, The Language of Emotions, focuses on how we can learn to access the astonishing genius in all of our emotions.

Understand Your Brain as a Predictor, Not a Reactor

Another old story about stress is that our brains react to the world: A stressor "happens," and our brains and bodies react without thought or choice. But researchers have understood for decades that our brains are predicting the future instead of reacting like hapless jack-in-the-boxes.

This predictive nature means that our brains are using our stores of past knowledge to help us make predictions and decisions about what may happen next.

If we believe outdated and damaging information about our stress responses, that bad information will become a self-perpetuating part of our predictions, and we'll misread our activation as a problem instead of a necessary part of preparation, resilience, and mastery.

When we have better information about stress, the values we hold, the importance of our strong stress responses, and the emotional truth hidden inside the weasel word of stress, we can reframe stress as necessary. And we can set ourselves up for better predictions in the future.

item.title: Thanksgiving Outside the Echo Chamber
item.description:
Theory of Mind

Thanksgiving Outside the Echo Chamber

Why intellectual curiosity belongs at the holiday table.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Thanksgiving brings us face-to-face with people outside our political echo chambers.
  • Intellectual curiosity encourages us to explore how others arrived at their beliefs.
  • Asking questions and listening can help us revise our theories of other people’s minds.
  • We can empathize with someone’s experiences without agreeing with their political beliefs.

“Polarized” has been one of the most overused words to describe America's political climate, but it is increasingly being applied to school boards, neighborhoods, and even families as well. Affective polarization, or the growing dislike and distrust of people on the opposing side of the political aisle, has more than doubled in the U.S. since the late 1970s (Boxell et al., 2024). Many of us now surround ourselves with like-minded friends and partners, creating a world in which we watch news, follow influencers, and make friends with people who reinforce what we already believe. This all gets thrown out the window at Thanksgiving, when we leave the safety of our echo chamber and spend time with the family we didn’t choose but love anyway.

Historically, the weird uncle at the Thanksgiving table could be counted on to tell a few off-color jokes or ask a child to pull his finger. These offenses seem almost quaint now that a passing comment about politics or social justice can leave half the table questioning the moral character of the other half. This annual exercise ends in one of two ways: The dinner crescendos into an actual altercation with one side accusing the other of crimes against humanity, or everyone smiles politely, and then unloads their thoughts and feelings to their significant other on the ride home. I’d like to propose a third option: intellectual curiosity.

What if we approached a conversation with someone whose political beliefs we find baffling with a genuine interest in how they came to hold those beliefs in the first place? It is true that not all beliefs are equal (beliefs such as racial superiority are indefensible); however, many people come to believe something they consider logical based on their life experience. For example: free college for all. Imagine cutting into the turkey when one family member casually says free college could open doors for students whose families can’t afford an education, and another relative pipes up that that wouldn’t be fair. Eating slows, as everyone recognizes dinner just got awkward.

Rather than writing off the relative you disagree with, use this time to practice intellectual curiosity, or the desire to learn, explore new ideas, and better understand something, even when it challenges what we already believe. This requires a couple of steps. The first is to pause. Polarizing comments are often triggering, and people often get angry before anything else. Recognize the anger and then pause until the initial rush passes.

Next, commit to intellectual curiosity by asking instead of telling. In the free college example, this may mean replying with, “I’d like to hear more about that. What feels unfair to you?” And then sit back and actually listen. Make eye contact, don’t interrupt, and don’t prepare your next argument. Doing this requires the next step: using your Theory of Mind.

Theory of Mind is the ability to understand that others have thoughts, beliefs, desires, and intentions that differ from our own. Because we can’t open someone’s head and look inside, we don’t know what they're actually thinking, but we gather clues from what they say and how they act to develop a theory of their mind. Theory of Mind develops rapidly across childhood and adolescence and continues into adulthood. This doesn’t mean all adults are good at it; in fact, I’d argue that most aren’t. We're already using Theory of Mind when we judge our relatives. We're just doing it with very little information and potentially a great deal of bias. When someone opposes free college, we might immediately assume they're selfish or indifferent to disadvantaged students. That assumption is itself a theory of their mind. Asking questions allows us to gather better information and revise that theory. At the Thanksgiving table, this means trying to put yourself in their shoes and take their perspective.

Finally, we can muster empathy. We’ve asked questions, revised our theory of their mind (why they believe what they do), and we still disagree with them. That’s okay; we can hold our beliefs and still find space in our heart to empathize with theirs. To return to the free college debate, imagine that a relative shares that they had to graduate in 5 years rather than 4 because they worked two jobs to pay for their education. Despite this, it still took them 17 years and a lot of low-budget vacations to pay off their loans, a milestone they just recently celebrated. Suddenly the word “fair” hits differently. You empathize with their situation, although you may still retain your initial position.

By the end of the night, you may still find your uncle’s political beliefs baffling, but you’ll better understand how he came to hold them. Given how much time we spend speculating about the minds of people we disagree with, why not take advantage of having one sitting across the table from us? Ask a few questions, entertain the possibility that you’ve misjudged someone, and see where the conversation goes. You might even have a more pleasant ride home.

item.title: Anxiety, ADHD, or Both?
item.description:
ADHD

Anxiety, ADHD, or Both?

Understanding the overlap between ADHD and anxiety through women’s lived experiences.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • ADHD-related mental restlessness can resemble anxiety, making it easier to overlook in women.
  • ADHD and anxiety can coexist, so assessment should explore what drives overlapping symptoms.
  • Identifying and supporting ADHD may ease anxiety linked to daily executive functioning challenges.
  • Hormonal fluctuations can influence ADHD symptoms, adding to changes in attention and emotional regulation.
When your mind won’t slow down, is it anxiety, ADHD, or both?
Source: istock/AaronAmat

If your mind never seems to shut off, it’s easy to assume you have anxiety—but that may not be the full story. Those racing thoughts might be better explained by the mental hyperactivity of ADHD, the worry that comes with anxiety, or both. The distinction may not feel useful when you’re overwhelmed and just need relief. But if you’ve been trying to manage anxiety and still struggle to keep up, understanding what’s behind those experiences matters—especially for women whose ADHD has gone unrecognized while their struggles have been labeled as being anxious, scattered, or “too emotional.”

How ADHD Can Be Mistaken for Anxiety

For some women, the path to an anxiety diagnosis begins with the strain of managing unrecognized ADHD. Difficulties with organization, planning, remembering, and following through create repeated experiences of falling behind. Over time, anticipating those struggles can bring worry about what might be forgotten or how everyone’s expectations will be met.

By the time a woman seeks support, worry, restlessness, irritability, and sleep disruption may be her most pressing concerns. It makes sense that anxiety becomes the focus. But without exploring what came before it, the difficulties contributing to that anxiety may remain unexplored:

Unrecognized ADHD → chronic overwhelm → persistent activation and worry → anxiety identified while ADHD remains overlooked

The anxiety is real, but does it tell the whole story?

So, Which Is It?

With ADHD, mental restlessness can involve moving quickly between ideas, distractions, and things you’re trying to remember. When keeping up takes considerable effort, that mental activity may become urgent: sorting through competing thoughts, remembering what needs to happen, or finishing something before attention shifts. It can feel overwhelming without necessarily beginning with fear.

Anxiety is more focused on fear, worry, or anticipating a negative outcome. With generalized anxiety, concerns can extend across many areas of life. Anxiety may show up mentally through persistent worry and physically through tension, a racing heart, or difficulty settling.

ADHD thoughts may shift rapidly between topics, while anxious thoughts often return to the same concern or feared outcome. These patterns offer clues rather than firm dividing lines. ADHD-related difficulties can give someone plenty to worry about, while anxiety can make attention and organization harder. The two also commonly co-occur. In one U.S. population study, nearly half of adults age 18-44 with ADHD also met criteria for an anxiety or related disorder in the previous year.

Anxiety as Scaffolding

One question worth asking is, “Does worry help me function?” This may seem odd when the goal is to feel less anxious. But for some women with ADHD, worry has become a way of staying on top of demands. Mentally rehearsing what needs to happen and anticipating what might be forgotten can feel protective. Relaxing, meanwhile, can feel risky, as though something might fall through the cracks.

Anxiety can become a form of scaffolding, helping to hold daily life together when other supports are missing. Internalized pressure may help initiate a task, while repeatedly checking work can become a way to catch missed details. Over time, it can be difficult to imagine functioning without that constant vigilance.

This doesn’t mean anxiety is necessary for managing ADHD. It invites a closer look at what worry has been helping accomplish—and what could replace it.

When the Coping Becomes the Cost

Overcompensation is one reason women with ADHD may be overlooked, as appearing “normal” can hide the effort and stress involved. Some may arrive everywhere early to compensate for time blindness—difficulty sensing how much time has passed or estimating how long things will take—while sacrificing time for their own needs.

The coping strategy becomes the cost.

Societal expectations to be productive at work, attentive at home, and responsible for everyone else’s needs add pressure. Those expectations also come with real work. The Pew Research Center found that in U.S. opposite-sex marriages where spouses earn roughly the same, wives spend approximately 4.6 hours weekly on housework compared with husbands’ 1.9 hours, while husbands have 25.2 hours of leisure time compared with wives’ 21.6. This reflects the “second shift”: unpaid household and caregiving work alongside paid employment.

For women with ADHD, those additional responsibilities mean more planning, organizing, and remembering, with less time to recover. Understanding that anxiety means considering both executive functioning difficulties and how much a woman is expected to manage.

Your Cycle May Also Offer Clues

If certain weeks feel harder than others, hormonal changes may contribute, particularly during the luteal phase, after ovulation and before the next menstrual period. Estrogen fluctuates during this phase and declines before menstruation. Emerging research links these fluctuations with changes in ADHD symptoms. This may partly reflect estrogen’s role in modulating dopamine signaling: As estrogen drops, changes in dopamine activity may affect attention and emotion regulation.

Greater difficulty focusing can increase anxiety about keeping up. Tracking attention, anxiety, sleep, and mood alongside the menstrual cycle can help identify patterns and guide treatment conversations. Hormonal changes can also make symptoms harder to navigate during puberty, postpartum, perimenopause, and menopause. A clinician familiar with hormonal influences on ADHD can help tailor treatment, including considering cycle-based dosing—adjusting ADHD medication around the menstrual cycle—or other individualized medication adjustments during hormonal transitions, when appropriate.

Supporting What Is Underneath

If worry has been helping with remembering, preparing, or following through, it makes sense that letting go feels difficult—even if relying on it is not sustainable long-term.

Women-Centered ADHD Treatment (W-CAT) considers both underlying ADHD needs and how women have adapted to keep up. Treatment planning includes considering medication with a prescribing provider alongside recommended W-CAT skills: cognitive offloading—putting reminders and plans outside the mind—sharing responsibilities, and breaking tasks into manageable steps. These are paired with support for regulation, building self-compassion, and addressing distressing beliefs.

Some anxiety may ease as ADHD is better supported, while some may need its own treatment. Before expecting yourself to let go of worry, consider how much you’ve been asking it to hold—and what support you deserve in its place.

Portions of this post were adapted from my book, Powered by ADHD: Strategies and Exercises for Women to Harness Their Untapped Gifts, and my Women-Centered ADHD Treatment (W-CAT) training.

item.title: How to Cure the Grand Theft Auto-VI Craze: Get Kids Knitting
item.description:
Child Development

How to Cure the Grand Theft Auto-VI Craze: Get Kids Knitting

Research shows that arts, crafts and DIY activities can have psychological benefits.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • There is evidence that doing crafts and do-it-yourself activities can positively impact our mental health.
  • Children don’t just need their screens turned off; they need to be offered opportunities for self-expression.
  • Children say they want alternatives to screen time, especially when it lets them show off their talents.

Grand Theft Auto VI has been dominating the lives of gamers, young and old, since its arrival on November 19th. It can seem impossible for parents to resist the inertia that settles on kids as they spend dozens (hundreds) of hours in front of screens engaged in violent role-play. While there is no easy solution, with the holidays fast approaching and gift-giving on many parents' minds, maybe there is a quaint solution to this very technological problem. Knitting.

A few months ago I was presenting to an audience in northern Norway where I observed something odd. At least 10% of my audience were knitting. These weren’t church ladies with white hair and compression socks (what an awful stereotype but sadly one that is portrayed far too often in our popular culture). My audience of knitters comprised, instead, younger women and men who were listening attentively to what I was saying while occupying their hands with needles and skeins of yarn. Where it has become routine to put stress balls and fidget toys on conference room tables, here was a much nicer way to evoke calm. Even better, the repetition wasn’t a wasted act of self-flagellation. My audience was engaged in a creative activity that turned a ball of wool into gifts for children or casual sofa throws for lovers and friends.

Why don’t we teach children to knit anymore? For that matter, why has it become so rare to see a child whittling with a pocket knife, sewing, building a tree fort, painting their room, drawing a tree, or creating something that is three-dimensional, tactile? So few children experience a distraction that has purpose and a tangible outcome. Video games are the opposite. Time consuming with no discernible gain.

If this sounds like nonsensical nostalgia, it’s not. There is good reason to believe that one part of the solution to our children’s mental health crisis is to be found in encouraging them to do arts and crafts and other do-it-yourself (DIY) activities like woodwork and gardening. In a study of 18-24-year-olds recruited (ironically) online, those who were more engaged in extracurricular activities, including crafts, reported significantly lower risk for suicide and a greater sense of belongingness, two outcomes that are co-dependent.

That same pattern was found during the COVID-19 pandemic when some 3,725 adults were surveyed in the USA, with a clear pattern to the findings. Those who gardened, those who did woodwork, and those who immersed themselves regularly in arts and crafts all reported lower rates of mental health problems.

While we adults obviously see these benefits, our children may, if given the opportunity, tell us that having some fun activities to do that don’t involve screens is actually welcomed. That was the message from a 2022 report that included over 7,000 kids in Finland where, to be honest, being outdoors and working with one’s hands is more a part of the culture than in North America. Still, it seems that kids who are encouraged to engage in non-screen activities can realize a nice mental health bump.

I can certainly relate to these findings. I’ve always been someone who liked to work with my hands. I am an avid woodworker, but also knit, sew and draw. I can remember well the feeling as a child of accomplishing something concrete and sharing it with others. The reflected glory of being seen as a maker was wonderful.

It’s up to us adults to not just take screens away from kids but to also provide the resources to keep them occupied. That might be an easel and paint, a saw and workbench, a garden or maybe a pet. And yes, it could even be a set of knitting needles and some brightly colored yarn.

item.title: The Boon of Being Highly Sensitive
item.description:
Highly Sensitive Person

The Boon of Being Highly Sensitive

High sensory sensitivity comes with strengths that can promote flourishing.

Posted November 24, 2026

Are you more easily overstimulated than others by what’s going on around you? Maybe you’re easily distracted or stressed by loud noises (it’s the kitchen exhaust fan for me), bright artificial lighting, uncomfortable clothing, or other people’s moods. If so, you may be among the 30% of people who are highly sensitive to sensory input from the environment.

We all navigate the world using our senses. It’s just that some of us seem to take in more and be more impacted by what we take in. Scientists are still making discoveries about sensory processing in different situations and for different people.

Here’s a fascinating example — did you know that human hands can sense the presence of something without touching it? Last year, a group of researchers published the first study demonstrating remote sensing in humans (Chen, Crucianelli, Versace, & Jamone, 2025). Participants in their study were able to detect that an object was buried in sand when their fingers were still 6.9 cm away from the object. How? Humans can perceive subtle changes in the sand caused by the object. What’s even more incredible is that humans were 30% more accurate than robotic sensors. Specifically, the robotic sensors had more false positives (“sensing” an object when there was not one). The researchers suspect humans are better able to interpret touch sensations because our nervous systems are designed to filter noise, weigh uncertainty, and make decisions about ambiguous situations.

Clearly, there's still a lot to learn about sensory processing in humans. These days, it’s widely accepted that some of us are more sensitive to the environment than others. As we understand more about sensory sensitivity, more research is focusing on an idea intuitive to many of us: sensory processing sensitivity comes with great benefits.

What Is Sensory Processing Sensitivity?

Dr. Elaine Aron began researching sensory processing sensitivity (SPS; also called high sensitivity) in 1991. SPS is well summarized as “lower sensory thresholds, susceptibility to overstimulation, deeper processing of environmental information, heightened emotional and physiological reactivity, and increased awareness of subtle stimuli” (Weyn, Greven, Schmidt, Gillebert, 2025).

SPS isn't a diagnosis. It's a normally distributed personality trait or aspect of temperament. This means we all fall somewhere on the sensitivity continuum. While 20-30% of us are highly sensitive, 40-50% of us are moderately sensitive, and 20-30% of us have low sensitivity (Lionetti et al. 2018). Evolutionary theories suggest there is an advantage for humans if some of us (not too many) are highly sensitive (Greven et al. 2019).

Sensory sensitivity is heritable. Studies have found that 47% of the variability in sensory sensitivity is explained by genetics (Assary, 2020). It’s also biologically based. Neuroimaging studies have found that folks with SPS have greater activation in brain areas involved in sensory processing (e.g., awareness, integration, empathy, preparation for action, higher-order visual processing).

Sensory processing sensitivity is typically measured using the Highly Sensitive Person Scale, which was revised earlier this year (Pluess et al. 2026). It's an 18-item questionnaire that captures six domains of sensitivity: 1. sensitivity to details 2. depth of processing 3. social sensitivity 4. sensitivity to positive experiences 5. emotional reactivity and 6. overstimulation.

If you (or someone you’re close to) has high sensory sensitivity, you don’t need me to tell you about its challenges, which can include overstimulation, exhaustion, and stress. What might not be top of mind are the benefits that can come along with high SPS. You may be surprised to learn that folks who have high SPS may actually be better positioned to thrive in supportive, positive environments (Damatac et al. 2025).

Sensitivity to Positive Experiences

If you’re someone who is more easily overstimulated by unpleasant sensory input like the kitchen fan, you’re likely also more easily positively influenced by positive input such as a view of the gorgeous fall leaves. And the positive benefit is likely to be longer-lasting. This makes logical sense. It’s also been supported by the research. In one example, Lionette et al. (2018) found that folks who had high SPS had a more positive response to happy video clips as compared with people who had lower sensory sensitivity. Research has also found that folks with high SPS can actually experience more benefit from psychological interventions and social support as compared with people with lower SPS (Damatac, et al. 2025; Nocentini, Menesini, & Pluess 2018).

This sensitivity to positive experiences overlaps with another dimension of SPS — aesthetic sensitivity. Aesthetic sensitivity describes the deep emotional and physiological response to beauty, art, and nature often experienced by folks who are highly sensitive.

Cognitive Flexibility and Adaptive Coping

Chacón et al. (2024) found aesthetic sensitivity among folks with high SPS strongly correlated with the personality traits openness and agreeableness (a replication of previous findings), as well as adaptive coping strategies including emotional expression and regulation. They found that folks with high SPS and high aesthetic sensitivity more effectively navigated emotionally dysregulating challenges in daily living, such as problematic situations at work.

Another recent study found that folks with sensory sensitivity demonstrated higher cognitive flexibility, which is associated with adaptive coping and problem-solving (Shippers, Hoogman & Greven, 2025). The study also found that folks with high SPS who were more sensitive to aesthetic beauty scored higher on measures of curiosity and humor.

Creativity, Empathy, and Awe

If you’re highly sensitive, you're likely more inclined toward creativity and empathy. Laros-van Gorkom et al. (2025) found that folks with high sensory sensitivity are more likely to be more empathic and more likely to have creative ideas. In their study, folks with high aesthetic sensitivity were more likely to engage in creative activities.

Those of us who have high sensory sensitivity experience awe more frequently. For example, Dunne et al (2024) found that folks with high SPS were more likely to experience a profound emotional and physiological response to the beauty of nature. This experience of awe directs attention away from ourselves and toward our natural surroundings, which deepens our connection to the natural world. The experience of awe is widely known to enhance well-being.

This rally around the advantages of SPS is extremely encouraging. It confirms that sensory sensitivity can be a strength promoting well-being. In positive environments, folks with SPS are actually uniquely positioned to flourish.
