item.title: "What Does This Mean For Me?" When Life Is All About Ourself
item.description:
Relationships

"What Does This Mean For Me?" When Life Is All About Ourself

Making ourselves the center of the universe does not make us happy.

Posted November 24, 2026

This is part 2 in a series. You can read part 1 here.

We don't interact with our life directly; we interact with what life means about us. What if the problem isn't that life isn't meeting our needs? What if the problem is that getting our personal needs met has become the single focus of our life?

Source: AI Generated Image

In part 1 of this series, I discussed the many ways we’re conditioned and wired to be self-focused in today’s world, to constantly monitor and manage our own okay-ness and whether our needs are being met. And furthermore, how each moment is experienced as what we've decided it says about us. Does this situation, conversation, decision, opinion make me feel less than or better than? Does it make me feel valued, comfortable, seen? Does it validate my story of “who I am”? I posited the idea that viewing our lives through the lens of “does this serve me?” is, at its root, an attempt to be happy, shore ourselves up, and ultimately, survive. While, in fact, we’ve got it wrong: putting “me” at the center of the universe and the reason everything happens ends up making us suffer.

So what exactly is the suffering that comes with our relentless self-focus—what’s wrong with seeing everything through the lens of how it affects “me”?

To name a few:

Emotional fragility. Defensiveness.

When we experience every situation and everyone else's choices through the lens of “self,” as fundamentally a commentary on how we're doing and a referendum on our worth, then every moment carries the potential to wound, undermine, humiliate, and destroy us. Every interaction can threaten who we think we are. We have to remain hyper-vigilant, therefore, on high alert for whether we’re okay or not okay, and any experience that feels like it doesn’t support our story of ourselves, which can also include a simple difference of opinion.

Emotional insatiability and dissatisfaction.

We live in a constant state of “not-enoughness.” We can never get enough approval, recognition, validation, reassurance, success, or reflection. The self that needs to be continually affirmed is never permanently satisfied; whatever we “get” only lasts as long as this particular experience. We imagine that if we win this argument or get this situation to “go our way,” and be “good for us,” we’ll finally get enough affirmation, enough validation to trust our worth and put down our “me” sword. But it never happens; there is no “enough” point, and so we live in a constant state of lack, always trying to get what we need from the outside so we can be okay on the inside.

The endless project of “me.” Self-management and self-improvement become an unending pursuit.

Our life becomes an endless project dedicated to self-management.

We feel like we have to be constantly improving the project of "me"—making sure we're doing enough and getting enough. Our life becomes a full-time job of managing the person we're trying to be and be seen as. The result is utter exhaustion and burnout.

We can’t be truly curious—about other people or the world.

Because we experience other people as threats to our self-story, and see others through the lens of whether their behavior serves or doesn’t serve us, we can’t meet people for real, as they are. We’ve got too much skin in the game. Who they are becomes about who they make us feel we are. And so, we can’t really relax fully and get to know others and give them the space to be who they are as whole beings, independent from us, with their own motivations, desires, wants, and needs that are not about us. All roads lead back to us in some way, which clouds our view of the other. We can’t really listen because we have to constantly monitor and scan for potential threats to who we are. We can’t allow others to have a different opinion or experience from us because it “means” our opinion is wrong and consequently, there’s something wrong with us. Our “me” agenda requires everyone else’s thoughts, opinions, and truth to confirm and align with our “me” project, which is a lot of work since that’s never the case. That said, only some parts of other people are allowed into our relationships, the parts that work for us and give us what we need. But we’re not available to meet or know the whole of them.

Our relationships are, therefore, built on filling our own holes and reassuring our own insecurities—getting what we need to feel good or at least okay. We end up using other people to satisfy and validate ourselves. We give in order to feel appreciated and be valued as helpful. We listen to others in order to be perceived as a good listener and so that we can be listened to. How we relate is driven by how it relates to and reflects on us. Our relationships, therefore, can’t be truly open, honest, and emotionally intimate; we can’t be vulnerable and undefended, and can’t really know others as people in their own right, who they really are separate from us. We remain disconnected, relating to others as merely supporting characters in our personal movie—the movie playing in our me-focused mind.

We don’t live in our life and don’t experience life as it is. We live in our interpretations about life, and specifically, what our life says about us.

Because we’re always telling ourselves a story about our life, what it means for us, whether we’re getting what we need, and whether our life is serving the project of “me,” we’re not available to life as it’s actually happening. We’re not in the present moment; we're trapped inside a story we’ve told ourselves about our life and how our “me” is faring in it. At the same time, we’re not truly connected to other people. Other people are characters in our personal movie, and are experienced through the lens of whether they’re filling our needs and making us feel good about ourselves. Other people are not subjects in their own right, but objects who can help support who we think we are.

Our self-focused approach to life is an attempt to keep us happy and secure, but it ends up backfiring, leaving us feeling disconnected from life and other people, enslaved to how we're being perceived. It leaves us defensive and emotionally fragile, vulnerable to other people’s different opinions and experiences, and having to constantly manage the project of “me” and make sure we’re enough.

In part 3, I’ll dive into the profound benefits of dropping “me” from the center of our universe, and the relief that comes when we learn to show up for life without our “me” in the way, and when we can see life as something happening, but without turning it into something happening to, for, and because of us. What if it’s not about us?

item.title: Why We Work So Hard… and What It Costs Us
item.description:
Career

Why We Work So Hard… and What It Costs Us

How the work ethic we inherited keeps us from the closeness we crave.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Most of us learn to put our faith in hard work as a way to build a secure future.
  • Our inherited work ethic can make work the centerpiece of our identity, at the cost of our relationships.
  • We can learn to value work and, when someone walks into the room, set it down and turn toward them.
Source: mixetto / iStockphoto

I was home recently, in the house I grew up in, for the first time since Mom died a few months earlier. I could feel her absence in my remembered expectations: I'd anticipate her coming down the hallway any moment now, her whole face lighting up as she spotted me around the corner; I'd open the fridge, prepared for it to be overflowing with my favorite foods, bought in anticipation of my homecoming; as dinner approached, I'd brace myself for her questions about what she could cook for me, or what she should order from Jerry's Pizzeria, a hometown staple and our family's favorite for over 50 years, and, of course, I'd look at the backgammon board sitting near the dining room table, waiting for her eager arrival and her excited Ready to play?, followed by her endless, playful attempts to cheat as the game wore on. (Mom, you can't cover the dice after you roll them!)

But other parts of her absence were more subtle, more internal…

With Mom, there were always two things alive at once. The first was her deep longing for connection and closeness, expressed through food and play and hug after hug after hug. (Mom called them fasses, her own made-up word; Come, let me fass you! she'd say, and then she’d squeeze you with all her might.) This part of her was born in the family village she grew up in, parents, uncles, aunts, and cousins all sharing one apartment building, filling her childhood with people who belonged to each other.

The second part awake in her was her fierce determination to see that I had a secure future, safe and stable, with the financial freedom to enjoy my life. Mom believed that kind of future would be earned through effort and hard work.

I took in both, and now, with her gone, I was giving myself the chance to sort through what I'd inherited: What did I want to keep, and what might I, at long last, set down? It's a reckoning many of us share…

A Shared Inheritance

Most parents, like Mom, love their children dearly and want to see them build a secure future. In a Pew Research Center survey (Minkin & Horowitz, 2023), 88 percent of American parents said it was extremely or very important that their children be financially independent as adults. No wonder so many of us grow up hearing some version of the same message: Build a secure life, and work hard to get there.

As young children, we comply with our parents’ priorities, believing that if we do what they ask, if we work hard, we’ll keep them near (Haines & Schutte, 2023).

That’s what I did. Early on, I put my faith in hard work as the way to ensure Mom stayed close… but not long after, I began noticing its limits. Sure, a new achievement brought a burst of applause, and a bigger accomplishment came with a trip to Classics Bookstore to pick out any book I wanted (I usually chose a Marvel graphic novel), but the celebration, and the closeness that came with it, never lasted long enough.

Still, I kept going, certain that the next achievement would bring what the last one hadn't, caught in what Tal Ben-Shahar (2007) calls the arrival fallacy: the belief that one day I’d accomplish a goal that would finally bring lasting closeness with Mom.

I’m still working hard today, and, if I'm being honest, I'm still caught in a version of that same arrival fallacy, a part of me believing hard work will accomplish some magical goal that will draw loving people near me (…and research suggests I’m far from the only one [Ben-Shahar, 2007]).

What Work Gives, and What It Takes

Now, with Mom gone, I find myself thinking about work. It's more than just ruminating on Too much work is bad, or wishing Mom hadn't taught me to work so darn hard. It's a deeper look back: Which part of my longing to do meaningful work was mine all along, and which part of my work ethic was handed to me at an early age and swallowed whole? Which parts of this life of hard work do I really want to keep, because it genuinely gives me something, and which parts do I want to change, because it takes more than it could ever give back?

I know work can be good for us. As social psychologist Marie Jahoda (1982) explained, beyond a paycheck, work gives us structure to our days, a sense of purpose, connection with other people, an identity, and regular activity, all important contributors to our well-being (Paul et al., 2023). I’ve felt every one of them, and I want to hold on to these parts.

But there comes a point where work stops giving and starts taking. For me, the real cost was that I had raised work above nearly everything else, even above time with the people I love… missing out on the very thing I’d hoped work would bring me in the first place. Writer Derek Thompson (2019) calls this workism, the transformation of work into the centerpiece of identity and purpose, often coming at the cost of relationship.

But my hard work wasn't only costing me relationship. It was also masking the loneliness I felt in its absence. In all the busyness and commotion and commitments that work brought, there was no time to feel the isolation I'd carried since childhood: I grew up with a Mom who loved me deeply, but who was stretched so thin by the tasks of everyday life that I was alone far more than I wanted to be. I grew up lonely, and from an early age, the busyness created by hard work spared me from feeling it.

What’s Worth Keeping

So, what will I keep? I’ll keep working, but I want my work to be less rigid and more organic, trusting that when someone walks into my room, or my life, I can set the work down and turn toward them… rather than keep them waiting because “Work matters most of all.” Deep down, I know the research is spot on: Belonging is a fundamental human need (Baumeister & Leary, 1995), and two million years of living in small, close-knit bands have wired us to want nothing less. It’s time I move further toward it.

I think Mom wants that for me too, sharing myself with the world, not just through what I do, but through how I show up for others in this life.

item.title: Why Do We Keep Gifts From Our Exes?
item.description:
Jealousy

Why Do We Keep Gifts From Our Exes?

What a new partner may make of your ex's sweater still in your closet.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • In a preliminary study, about seven in ten women and men had kept items from a past relationship.
  • Some keepsakes bothered new partners more than others, and sex toys were the least welcome.
  • The motive mattered most, and "It is a memory" landed better with partners than lingering attachment.

With the holidays fast approaching, many of us might be thinking of what to give our partner. Or maybe we are thinking about what special present our partner will give us. What we probably do not want to consider is that the gift, which initially brings joy, may outlast our actual relationship. This made me start to wonder—once the relationship ends, do you keep the gift, or do you toss it away? And do you tell a new partner that the item was from an ex, and if so, how do you explain why you are keeping it?

How Common Is Keeping Gifts From an Ex?

In a preliminary study, my research team asked 83 heterosexual adults in the United States what items they kept from a past romantic relationship, and why they had hung onto them. What we did not expect was how many people kept items. In our sample, 71 percent of women and 72 percent of men said they kept things, with clothing and jewellery the most common. What was also interesting were the reasons for keeping items; women reported being more sentimental, saying they wanted to keep the gift because of the memories, while men were more practical, saying they kept items because they were useful.

Why would someone hang onto something? One evolutionary psychological study by Saad and Gill (2003) proposes that gifts are a way for a potential mate to show their romantic interest and commitment and to signal that they have resources. If correct, then keeping a gift from an ex might remind us that somebody once thought we were worth the effort, and I suspect that reminder is hard to throw in the trash.

But how did new partners feel about it? We performed a short follow-up survey of 76 heterosexual adults in the United States who were in a relationship to imagine that their new partner had kept some items from an ex. Not surprising was that some items bothered new partners more than others. A sweater was not a big deal, but a sex toy bothered about half. Photos were an issue for about a third of respondents. The figure includes our preliminary findings.

Share of respondents who said they would be somewhat or very uncomfortable if their current partner kept each item from an ex. Preliminary results from 71 adults in a relationship.
Source: Maryanne Fisher

What matters the most, though, was the motive behind keeping the item, as it provides a window into one’s current relationship status. When the explanation revolved around it being part of a memory, most people (59 percent) said they would be comfortable with the item, while 17 percent said they would be uncomfortable. An explanation that an item was useful was likewise seen by about half (54 percent) of respondents as a comfortable reason. Not surprisingly, when the explanation reflected unfinished business with an ex, new partners grew increasingly uncomfortable. Saying that one wanted to keep an ex’s gift because they were not ready to move on or still felt attached to the ex led a third of respondents (29 percent) to say they were uncomfortable.

How Keepsakes From an Ex Can Trigger Jealousy

Evolutionary psychology also provides a possible explanation for why a new partner might be uncomfortable. Jealousy is often described as an alarm that sounds when a rival threatens a valued relationship, and an ex is the most obvious rival. Research shows a large number of people get back together with an ex; in one study of young adults in the United States, 44 percent had broken up and reconciled with their current or most recent partner (Halpern-Meekin et al., 2013), and some research suggests it is more than 60 percent (Dailey et al., 2009). That item might matter if it hints to a new partner that the ex is still in the running.

We also found a sex difference, with men being generally more uncomfortable with a new partner hanging onto any keepsake for any reason. Men also tended to keep items only if the ending was a good one, but they tossed items from a bad breakup. Women, in contrast, were much more likely to keep an item, even after a breakup ended badly. Why would men and women differ? At this point, I can offer some speculated answers. Maybe men tend to be more upset than women by the sexual side of a partner’s infidelity, and a keepsake from an ex is a daily reminder that there was someone before. Men are also the ones who more often give gifts as a courtship tactic, which may make them quicker to see another man's gift as a rival’s investment. As for women keeping items even after a bad ending, a costly gift (like jewellery) holds its value no matter how the relationship ended. In addition, if the item is kept for the memories, as women told us in our first study, those memories are part of her own life, which a bad breakup does not take away. A necklace kept for the memories is a souvenir of a period in the keeper’s life, reflecting where she lived, who she was, and what that year felt like. That period happened and is part of her story, whether the relationship ended kindly or horribly; perhaps a bad breakup changes how she feels about the ex, but it does not erase the memories that came before.

A new partner might not care much about that worn red sweater in your closet, but they will care about whether the ex that gave it to you still has a spot in your heart that is unresolved. If the honest answer is that it was a memory, a moment in time, and that there is nothing that remains unfinished, keep the sweater and enjoy it. If the honest answer is yes, the sweater is not going to be your biggest problem.

item.title: Watching 'The Wiz' Is Both Tradition and Medicine
item.description:
Awe

Watching 'The Wiz' Is Both Tradition and Medicine

The ancestral intelligence in a favorite holiday tradition.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Watching "The Wiz" together is a collective nervous system reset.
  • Chosen family counts. The nervous system does not distinguish between blood and safety.
  • Singing, dancing, and laughter are medicine.
Source: Any Lane / Pexels

I don’t know about your family, but every holiday season starting in November and ending January 1st, my family is definitely watching "The Wiz"; it’s a family tradition. In fact, it’s a tradition for many Black families across America. We pile onto sofas, sing, dance, cry, and debate, and it is tradition. But it also is medicine.

"The Wiz" has been healing Black families since 1978. Science is just now catching up to what your grandmother already knew.

What Your Nervous System Is Doing During the Opening Credits

When your family settles in for a ritual you have done together before—the same movie, the same couch, the same debates about the same scenes—your nervous system registers something specific: safety. Predictable shared experience signals to the brain that threat is low and belonging is high. Oxytocin, the neurochemical of trust and bonding, is released during group ritual. Cortisol drops. The vagus nerve, the body’s primary regulation highway, begins to settle. This is not metaphor; it is the physiology of communal gathering, and families have been administering it with precision for decades.

Why the Singing Is the Intervention

When “You Can’t Win” comes on and you sing along, loud and proud and probably off-key, you are activating your vagus nerve directly. Humming, chanting, and singing stimulate the vagal branches in the throat and chest in ways that measurably increase heart rate variability, the primary marker of nervous system regulation. Group singing amplifies this effect. Research shows that people who sing together synchronize their heart rates. Your family is not only performing. They are co-regulating.

Add in the dancing—spontaneous, in your living room, because you cannot help it when “Brand New Day” comes on and you have activated somatic release. Movement is one of the most effective tools we have for discharging stored stress from the body. Bessel van der Kolk spent a career documenting what dancers and African traditional healers demonstrated before the research did: The body holds what the mind cannot process, and movement releases it.

On Laughter and the Immune System

There is always a moment in "The Wiz" when someone in your family loses it completely. The tears, the laughter, every time; this is not weakness. Shared laughter measurably reduces cortisol, increases natural killer cell activity, and produces documented improvements in immune function. Laughter researcher Lee Berk at Loma Linda University has been publishing on this for decades. Your family’s annual hysteria over the crows or flying monkeys is a clinical-grade immune intervention.

The Awe Response

When Dorothy finally gets home, when the music swells, and Lena Horne sings “Believe in Yourself,” and everyone starts crying before the scene even finishes because we have seen it 20 times and it still does this to us; what is happening is awe. Psychologist Dacher Keltner at UC Berkeley has documented awe as one of the most powerful mental health interventions identified in contemporary science. Awe reduces self-focused thinking, increases prosocial behavior, and produces measurable reductions in inflammatory markers. And because awe almost always arrives alongside emotional release—the tears, the full-body exhale, the feeling of being cracked open in the best possible way—it also completes what the dancing started. The body finishes processing what it has been carrying. Your tears are data. Your relief is the point.

The Ancestral Layer

"The Wiz" is not just a movie. It is a Black retelling of the oldest story we tell: the journey home to self, to community, to wholeness. Dorothy is doing identity reclamation. The Scarecrow is reclaiming his mind. The Lion is reclaiming his courage. The Tin Man is reclaiming his heart. Our ancestors told this story in circles, around fires, through spirituals. "The Wiz" put it on a screen in 1978, in full Black excellence, and handed it to us as a holiday tradition.

When elders and children watch it together, something else happens. Cultural identity, racial socialization, and connection to Black heritage and community are documented protective factors against the mental health effects of racism. Annual Review of Clinical Psychology research confirms that ethnic and racial identity functions as a clinical buffer. Intergenerational storytelling is not nostalgia. It is immunization.

What to Do With This Information

If "The Wiz" is already your tradition, protect it. Deepen it. Tell your children what is actually happening when you all pile onto that couch. If you lost the tradition somewhere along the way, bring it back this holiday season. If you never had it, start it this year.

Watch it alone if you have to. Let Diana Ross, Michael Jackson, Nipsey Russell, Ted Ross, and Lena Horne be your circle. In my work on public health and ancestral healing, and in my book Ancestral Roots, I return again and again to the truth that chosen family is real family. Your nervous system does not distinguish between blood and chosen. It only knows safety, belonging, and joy.

"The Wiz" delivers all three. Every single time.

item.title: Women Aging Well: Lessons From Memories and Reflections
item.description:
Aging

Women Aging Well: Lessons From Memories and Reflections

Reflection and remembrance can help us reconnect with what matters most.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Reflecting on meaningful memories can deepen our awareness of love and connection.
  • Mindful attention can help us notice thoughts and feelings without immediately judging them.
  • As we age, we can reconsider how we spend our time and what deserves more of our attention.
  • Making room for love and kindness can bring greater intention to our later years.
Dale Standing in Front of the Labyrinth
Source: Dr. Dale Atkins

In Tennessee, I walked a magnificent labyrinth inspired by a clock, formed with 1,000 feet of stone, designed as a space of reflection and connection. The artist, Thea Alvin, titled her installation "Time for Love." Since I’ve been thinking about the importance of time as we age, I wandered slowly and quietly on the spiral path toward its center, open to whatever thoughts and feelings emerged. Immediately I relaxed, knowing I would arrive at the center, stay a while, and return along the same path.

As I get older, I am more aware that the path in is never the same as the path out. No path is ever the same because of changes in weather, light, time of day, and the path itself. I am not the same. Just as we can never step in the same river twice, we can never walk along the same path because neither we nor the path remain the same. We evolve over time; as we age, we are continuously unfolding and hopefully, moving toward self-discovery and a center of calm.

Evolution and Transformation

I experienced entering the labyrinth as an opportunity to be open and curious about my life at this moment. I have always been drawn to spiral shapes as they are often associated with evolution and transformation. As a nature lover, I notice spiral shapes of pinecones, sunflowers, and other life forms. As I walked the spiral path, I heard the wind, the birdsongs, and the crunching gravel underneath my feet. I listened deeply to myself, without judgment or criticism. When a thought or feeling surfaced, I attempted to observe it and see what it meant. I stayed with that thought and waited to see what else emerged. These were my mind’s musings as I walked to the center. Cultivating curiosity and willingness to stay with a thought or feeling as we age can help us deepen awareness about ourselves, our relationships, and hopefully, encourage us to examine the choices we make in our daily lives.

Reminisce as Comfort

At the center, I sat on a boulder under a Beech tree, contemplating "Time For Love." The structure was commissioned as a space for family members to come, sit, and remember their loved one who died. The place feels sacred. In my reflection, I recalled people and pets I’ve loved over the course of my life. I felt the warmth of those memories. I realized how much I enjoy reminiscing in this way; quietly, in nature, experiencing sadness and joy. As Thea Alvin intended, I was allocating "Time for Love." Noticing an internal shift, I recognized the necessity of giving myself this time for reflection on love. I needed to do this, and asked myself: How do I use my time compared to how I want to spend it?

Reflection on Time Past and Present

Those questions stayed with me as I walked out of the labyrinth. I realized that this thought was not just inspired by the labyrinth but also by Varun Soni, Dean of Religious Life at USC, who spoke at a conference I attended about children and spirituality. He asked: “What deserves more of our attention?” “What would we like to make room for?” “What small change regarding our time could we make today?”

Create Time for Love

These are important questions to consider at any age; particularly when we are in our older years, when we are more aware of the time that has passed in relation to the time we may have ahead. The final question Dean Soni asked was “What can we do to change what we discover?” Sitting on a rock, under a tree, in the center of "Time for Love," I realized that I can dedicate time to feel the love that I had in my life, and to actively cultivate the love that I feel now. How will I make more time for love? I will remember those I loved; engage in activities I love, be with people I love, share love in ways that make others feel loved, and engage in acts of loving kindness.

As I returned along the spiral path, I felt different. I was different. I discovered that actively engaging with love deserves more of my time and attention. And in making this change, I will feel this connection to love as a vital, positive force in my own aging.

item.title: Make Gratitude the Main Course, Not the Side Dish
item.description:
Gratitude

Make Gratitude the Main Course, Not the Side Dish

New research reveals that gratitude has a wider reach than we might think.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • According to research, gratitude is one of the five most important character strengths for well-being.
  • Couples who express gratitude well have a greater chance of staying together.
  • When people witness gratitude in action, it signals warmth and trustworthiness.
Source: Tima Miroshnichenko / Pexels

With Thanksgiving approaching, many of us are busy planning our menus. Turkey or ham? Mashed or roast potatoes? Pumpkin or pecan pie?

While we may spend countless hours and enormous effort preparing the perfect meal, how much time do we invest in cultivating the emotion at the heart of the holiday?

Too often, gratitude is served up as a side dish—a brief expression of thanks before we dive into our feast. But what if we made gratitude the main course?

Why Gratitude?

Gratitude offers enormous benefits for our physical and mental health. Given its importance, we dedicate an entire chapter to it in our book, Happy Together: Using the Science of Positive Psychology to Build Love That Lasts, and have written about it here, here, and here.

According to positive psychology research, it is one of the five most important character strengths for individual well-being. Leading emotion scientist Barbara Fredrickson similarly argues that it’s vital to our relationships, noting that couples who express gratitude well have a greater chance of staying together.

The Ripple Effect of Gratitude

Recent research suggests that gratitude’s positive reach extends far beyond the two people directly involved.

In a paper published in Affective Science, researchers conducted two studies involving 680 participants. In the first study, participants watched a video of someone helping another person solve a problem. Afterward, the person who received help responded with either gratitude or simple positivity. Viewers then shared their personal impressions of that person. In the second study, participants had to decide whether to cooperate with the grateful person to earn money, even though doing so left them vulnerable to exploitation.

The researchers found that simply witnessing expressions of gratitude—rather than general positivity—fostered more favorable impressions of that person. In fact, it created a “halo effect” wherein participants felt greater trust, closeness, and willingness to interact with the grateful person, even when cooperating on a risky financial task. When people witness gratitude in action, it signals warmth and trustworthiness, creating opportunities to bring groups and communities together.

Pass the Gratitude

To build that same sense of trust, closeness, and community around your Thanksgiving table, try shifting how you share thanks this year.

  • Make it personal. Instead of simply going around the table and having everyone list what they’re grateful for, invite family and friends to express gratitude directly to one another—and explain why they’re grateful.
  • Focus on character. Be specific in spotlighting a strength or action that you appreciate about the person.
  • Be authentic. While gratitude is good for us, previous research has shown that disingenuous or exaggerated expressions can backfire.

This Thanksgiving, rather than just filling our plates, let’s also remember to focus on nourishing our relationships. Gratitude, it turns out, is a dish best shared—and its benefits may extend far beyond the people at the table.

item.title: How to Slowly Dissolve a Deep Fear of Intimacy
item.description:
Fear

How to Slowly Dissolve a Deep Fear of Intimacy

Undoing a fear of intimacy can be a slow but liberating process.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Many people struggle with anxieties that hinder their ability to form and sustain fulfilling bonds.
  • To address fears of rejection, objectively examine the evidence and avoid overinterpreting it with negativity.
  • The fear of abandonment can be rooted in past experiences of feeling left behind or neglected.
Source: Katerina Holmes / Pexels

Building and maintaining healthy connections requires individuals to be vulnerable, trust one another, and invest emotionally in the relationship. Unfortunately, many people struggle with anxieties that hinder their ability to form and sustain fulfilling bonds.

These relationship fears often stem from past experiences that have left emotional scars, deep-seated insecurities, or negative beliefs about oneself and relationships in general. While most people label their acquired fears and insecurities as a general "fear of intimacy," it can be worth diving deeper and picking apart the notions shaping this fear in the first place.

Not only will it help you be the best version of yourself in your relationship, but you will also be able to articulate your needs more precisely.

Here are three inherent fears you might have that could, over the years, develop into a larger, more amorphous fear of being intimate and vulnerable with someone.

1. Fear of Rejection

Fear of rejection can be a formidable barrier to building and nurturing relationships and might stem from the deep-seated, evolutionary anxiety of not being accepted or valued by others, which can lead to self-doubt. It can manifest in many ways, such as avoiding social situations, being overly self-conscious, or being excessively critical of oneself.

In research focusing on rejection, lead author and psychologist Mark Leary found that many people tend to perceive more rejection in their lives than they actually experience.

“We tend to have negative, rather than neutral, reactions to learning that someone feels neutral about us. What this means is that most people probably go through life feeling more rejected than they actually are,” he explains.

Therefore, if someone is experiencing feelings of rejection or struggling to feel accepted, it is important for them to consider whether they may be underestimating their worth in relationships due to ambiguous social cues or perceiving neutral feedback as negative. The initial step in addressing concerns about rejection is to objectively examine the evidence and avoid overinterpreting it with negativity.

Another way to avoid being controlled by your fear of rejection is to challenge your negative thoughts and embrace your self-worth through self-regulation.

Self-regulation is the ability to identify and control your emotions and behaviors, which plays a key role in challenging negative thoughts that lead to feelings of fear and insecurity. Once you are aware of maladaptive thought patterns, you can reframe them by seeking evidence for your belief, consciously practicing positive self-talk in weak moments, and taking time to truly appreciate yourself.

2. Fear of Inadequacy

The fear of inadequacy or the belief that we are not deserving of a fulfilling relationship can take a heavy emotional toll on us. This fear can manifest in a number of ways, too, like constantly comparing yourself with others or your partner’s ex(es), or experiencing the lingering feeling of never being good enough.

A recent study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology suggests that reflecting on positive romantic experiences and simple acts of love and affection can accumulate to make both partners feel more secure in a relationship.

“When jointly reminiscing about these positive experiences, partners can try to validate one another and the relationship. Telling how grateful they are for sharing the experience, disclosing positive emotions they felt during the experience or expressing how much they look forward to similar experiences in the future can be reassuring,” state the authors.

3. Fear of Abandonment

The fear of abandonment can be rooted in past experiences of feeling left behind or neglected, creating a lingering fear of being alone or unloved in relationships. This fear can manifest in two ways:

  1. If you’ve been emotionally neglected in the past by parents, a caregiver, or a partner, you might fear that other people will neglect you too, causing fear of emotional abandonment.
  2. Physical abandonment happens when an important person exits your life abruptly. For example, you might live with fear of abandonment today that is connected to a parent leaving you in your childhood.

In fact, a study published in the Journal of Youth and Adolescence explains that the death of a parent can also lead to deeply entrenched abandonment issues, giving rise to anxiety in romantic relationships and even depressive symptoms as late as six years into the relationship.

To dilute the long-term impact unaddressed abandonment issues can have on your life, you can start by recognizing your triggers to manage your fears. Identify the situations, behaviors, or specific relationships that trigger your fear of abandonment.

For example, notice if your anxiety escalates during disagreements with your partner, or if you fear being replaced when you see them spending time with friends or engaging in activities without you.

Acknowledging your fear of abandonment might be the most difficult, but ultimately the most effective, step toward a life where you feel secure in your closest relationships.

Being propelled by your fears is possibly the most unsatisfying approach to living life. But this does not mean that you have to throw yourself into the deep end all the time. Slowly dismantling your fears and their underlying faulty cognitions can bring about a massive transformation in the way you view and behave in relationships.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: Building Confidence From Failure
item.description:
Resilience

Building Confidence From Failure

How you see your goal decides what failure does to you.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Tenzing Norgay was turned back from Everest six times before he reached the summit in 1953.
  • Failure tends to erode confidence unless we treat it as a sign of improvements we can make.
  • If you see a goal as a conquest, each setback is a defeat. See it as a request, and failure is just "not yet."
Source: fotogurme / Adobe Stock

There is something about summits that enthralls the human spirit. We build careers, companies, and identities around reaching our personal peaks or the summits of our industries. We put mountaintops on posters and gaze longingly at their beauty and remoteness. Yet in life, as in mountaineering, the summit may be the goal, but it is never the real story. Few people understood this better than Tenzing Norgay.

Seven Attempts

Tenzing grew up in the shadow of the Himalayas, herding yaks in the Khumbu, the craggy highlands below Everest. The mountain that loomed over his childhood—known to the locals as Chomolungma—would come to define his life.

As a teenager, Tenzing ran away to Darjeeling to look for work with the foreign expeditions that used the Indian city as a staging post for their journeys into the Himalayas. He started as a porter and rose to become a sirdar, the head Sherpa who recruits and leads an expedition's support team. In all, he spent nearly two decades carrying loads in pursuit of other people's dreams.

Inevitably, many of these foreigners were drawn toward Everest, and so Tenzing found himself working his way up the mountain again and again. He joined his first Everest expedition in 1935. In 1952, alongside the Swiss climber Raymond Lambert, he came within a few hundred meters of the top. The next year, on his seventh attempt, he finally reached the summit with the New Zealand climber Edmund Hillary.

Tenzing was by then in his late 30s. After nearly 20 years on the mountain, the difference between one more failed attempt and the chance to stand at the highest point on Earth came down to a single morning's climb. In truth, the journey had taken a lifetime.

Asking Permission

In the West, people spoke of the conquest of Everest. The mountain had not simply been climbed. It had been overcome, taken possession of by adventurous humans on an expedition mounted, significantly, by a great European empire. Tenzing, a devout Buddhist, knew better.

Chomolungma means "Holy Mother," and one does not conquer one's mother. Sherpas ask her for permission to climb, and when they succeed, they give thanks. When he reached the summit with Hillary, Tenzing's celebration was characteristically modest. He buried a few small offerings in the snow, among them sweets and a pencil his daughter had given him. For Tenzing, a mountain was not something to be overcome. One should approach it, he said, “as a child climbs onto the lap of its mother.”

It is easy to assume that Tenzing's humility and deference left no room for the striving ambition of the Western adventurers he so often accompanied. But it is a mistake to think that modesty and ambition are incompatible.

What Failure Does

Those other people's dreams were also Tenzing's own. He wrote that climbing Everest was what he had wanted most in his life, and six times the mountain turned him back.

For some people, that repeated experience of falling short of a deep personal goal would have undermined their confidence and self-belief. But failure does not have to be damaging. What matters is how we choose to interpret it. People with resilient confidence treat a failure as a learning experience, as evidence of a gap in their effort, knowledge, or skill set that can be closed. People who treat a failure as a verdict on who they are rarely learn anything from their setbacks except how to condemn themselves.

This is where Tenzing's way of holding his ambition mattered. If a mountain is an enemy to be conquered, then every retreat is a defeat, and six defeats amount to a judgment. If a mountain is a mother whose permission you ask, then a retreat means only that permission has not yet been given. Tenzing came down in 1952 knowing the route, knowing his own body at 28,000 feet, and knowing that the summit could be reached. He went back the following spring and asked again.

The View From Home

I grew up in Bangladesh, on the flat green delta where the great rivers of the Himalayas meet the sea. The water that fed our fields began as snow on those peaks, and Darjeeling, where Tenzing made his home, lies only a short distance beyond our northern border. For a boy on the delta, the mountains were a horizon, close enough to imagine yet too far to reach. Tenzing's story was part of that horizon: a poor boy with no formal schooling who kept going back until the mountain let him through.

I left Bangladesh at 17 and arrived in America with very little. In the late 1990s, I was building a startup, and like Tenzing, I teamed up with people who had the means to get me up the mountain. The venture capitalists who backed me saw the market as something to be conquered, and conquered quickly. They pushed for expansion at a rate the company could not sustain, and I went along with it, even as the pace forced compromises to the vision I had started with. Eventually we fell out, and I was pushed out of the business I had built. Over the next several years, I watched it fall apart.

For a long time, I treated that failure as if it was a defeat. It took me years to learn to view it in the same way Tenzing viewed his retreats from Everest. Tenzing had spent 20 years climbing beside people who spoke of conquest without ever taking on their view of the mountain. I had taken on my investors' view of the market and let it shape my own approach to business.

When I started again, my ambition was intact, and I still wanted to reach the top. What was different was how I climbed. Where I had once seen building a company as a battle to be waged against outside forces, I now saw it as a conversation with myself, with my teams, and with the markets and clients I hoped to serve. My part in that conversation was to ask and then to listen, even when the answer was no. Tenzing's mountain turned him back six times before it let him through. Mine have turned me away many times since, but I know now how to return.

item.title: To Help Children Cope With Loss, Begin With the End in Mind
item.description:
Parenting

To Help Children Cope With Loss, Begin With the End in Mind

How parents can support their child in coping with uncertainty and loss.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Pay attention to your child's response. Don't assume that your child is as upset as you are.
  • Join with your child's emotion before trying to respond or offer an explanation.
  • Help your child consider neutral consequences or opportunities can arise from initially undesirable events.

There are two wishes most parents have for their child. One is that nothing bad will happen to them. And the second is that if and when something does, they will be OK. Every parent knows that their first wish is impossible, and that their child will be disappointed or frustrated or experience some kind of negative emotion over the course of their life. So one of your tasks as a parent is to help your child develop the knowledge and capacity to emerge from these kinds of challenging moments essentially unharmed.

One experience that can be particularly unsettling, especially for younger children, is the sudden departure of a caregiver or teacher. Over the years, many parents have come to me wondering how best to support their child when a nanny or teacher leaves with little or no notice. Two aspects of a caregiver's sudden departure can be particularly distressing. The first is the loss of the connection, support, and caring provided by someone with whom the child has developed a significant relationship. The second may be uncertainty about why the person left.

These two aspects of the experience are not mutually exclusive. A child may miss the person who left while also feeling confused or wondering why they left or whether someone else might leave or disappear without warning. Parents may need to address both the emotional loss and the uncertainty, depending on how their child responds.

Source: SDI Productions / Getty Images Signature

Responding to Your Child

The first piece of advice I would give is to remember the end goal: for your child to be OK in spite of whatever difficult situation they may be facing. And while you may also be affected by the situation, disappointed by the loss or by what you imagine may come with this change, your child may not experience the situation in the same way. Pay attention to your child's response. Don't assume that your child is as upset as you are or understands the implications in the same way.

Join with your child's emotion before trying to respond or offer an explanation. Acknowledge what your child seems to be feeling. You might say, "I notice that you seem sad." You could also ask, "How do you feel about that?" particularly if your child's emotions are not apparent or obvious. Asking also indicates that you are open to talking about how the event has affected your child. When we don't discuss obvious topics, the elephant in the room, even the youngest children notice and may wonder whether it's a topic that is off limits. That's not the message you want to send your child, even if you don't know how to answer their questions or they ask something you don't want to answer.

Then, if your child has questions, let those questions guide the conversation. You don't need to share everything you know, worry about, or imagine to be true. Answer your child's questions at the level of interest they express, rather than at the level of knowledge you possess as a parent.

Helping Children Tolerate Uncertainty

In the absence of information, our default is often to imagine the worst. One caution, then, is to recognize that our own tendency to imagine the worst when we don't have all the information can influence what we communicate to our children. Children learn from what they observe, including how we respond to uncertainty.

If your child is going to the dark side with their assumptions or explanations for what has happened, help your child consider alternative explanations without inventing facts. An absence of information doesn't necessarily mean something terrible has happened. And one goal is for your child to be OK with ambiguity.

For instance, if your child worries that the caregiver left because of something they did, you can help them consider other possibilities without claiming to know the reason for the departure. You may also want to reassure your child that they are not responsible for the caregiver's departure, whether the adult chose to leave or someone else made that decision.

There is also the opportunity to practice tolerating uncertainty. Sometimes, no matter how much we think about what happened, we won't know why someone behaved as they did. There may be several possible explanations, and we may never know which one is correct. Learning to tolerate that uncertainty, rather than continuing to search for an answer that we will never be sure of, is an important skill.

You can decide, with each situation that presents itself, how much you want to engage in this kind of exercise and how deeply you want to explore it. Sometimes just acknowledging the uncertainty is enough. At other times, it may be helpful to consider several possible explanations. Not every disappointment can be explained away, and not every question will have an answer.

Source: dragana991 / Getty Images

Helping Children Manage the Emotional Loss

Even when a child understands what happened, they may continue to miss the person. Parents can offer emotional support while helping their child recognize that unpleasant feelings generally diminish over time. You can acknowledge that your child misses their teacher or nanny, talk about what they liked about that person, or just listen when they want to talk. None of these responses requires you to resolve the situation or make the sadness disappear.

Sometimes there isn't another explanation that makes the loss less painful. Sometimes there isn't a lesson to be learned. Sometimes the child just needs to feel sad and discover that they can tolerate those feelings.

There is also the normal response to disappointment. Do you read a book, talk to someone, reframe the situation, or acknowledge that the situation is painful and that the feeling will pass after a period of time? These are different strategies, and different strategies work for different situations at different times. What we want ideally is a repertoire of strategies that we can pull from. Tolerating an unpleasant feeling is itself an approach we can use to cope with unpleasant situations. Sometimes learning to tolerate an unpleasant feeling is in itself an accomplishment.

Source: mg7 / Getty Images

Conclusion

While parents may wish to protect their child from disappointment, what's probably more reasonable and helpful to your child in the long run is not to ensure that nothing disappointing ever happens, or even that your child never feels distressed. It is to help your child become increasingly capable of managing those experiences.
